the encroaching trees and the grasses are using the same sources of water, with the trees using a more plastic and opportunistic approach to soil water extraction, and with the grasses using more shallow soil water sources.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the grasses were shallow-rooted and extracted most of their soil water in the upper soil profile, while the trees were deep-rooted and extracted water from below 2 m depth, and that these patterns of water use were consistent with the species' life history strategies.

the grasses were less flexible in tracking the changes in soil moisture content with depth, whereas the trees exhibited plasticity in water uptake, which allowed them to use the water available in the soil profile, and thus maintain their transpiration rates and water potentials during drought periods.

trees are more efficient in tracking soil water availability in deep soil profiles than grasses and that this ability allows them to survive drought conditions and to persist in the Sandhills grassland.
The main takeaway from our work is that
trees and grasses have different patterns of soil water use, and these patterns are likely to change with changes in soil water availability and plant water demand.
the depth of water uptake is highly variable among tree species, and can vary seasonally.

the water use patterns of woody encroaching species are highly plastic and can be altered by seasonal changes in precipitation and soil water availability, and that the water uptake by woody species is not limited to the shallow soil profile as has been previously reported.
